Here is the overall argumentation strategy: Socrates aims to guide Meno towards understanding the requirements for a proper, universal definition of virtue by systematically eliciting, examining, and refuting Meno's inadequate initial attempts.
Here are the conceded premises: Bees do not differ from one another as bees., Virtues have a common nature that makes them virtues., Health, size, and strength are the same whether in a man or woman., Men and women must have the same virtues of temperance and justice to be good., All men are good in the same way, by participation in the same virtues., Virtue is the power of governing mankind, but must be done justly., Justice is 'a virtue', not 'virtue' itself., There are other virtues besides justice, such as courage, temperance, wisdom, and magnanimity.
Here is interlocutor profile: Meno's current claim is that virtue is 'the power of governing mankind,' which he has qualified with 'justly.' He is struggling to grasp the concept of a universal definition, tending to provide examples or parts of virtue rather than a common essence, but is willing to engage with Socrates' analogies and questions.
Here is the dialogue summary: Socrates used an analogy of 'figure' to clarify the distinction between a universal definition and a list of examples, leading Meno to concede that justice is 'a virtue' rather than 'virtue' itself. Socrates then asked Meno to list other virtues, which Meno did, leading Socrates to point out that they are still searching for the common nature of virtue.
Here are the last lines of dialogue:
Socrates: Would you say "virtue," Meno, or "a virtue"?
Meno: What do you mean?
Socrates: I mean as I might say about anything; that a round, for example, is "a figure" and not simply "figure," and I should adopt this mode of speaking, because there are other figures.
Meno: Quite right; and that is just what I am saying about virtue-that there are other virtues as well as justice.
Socrates: What are they? tell me the names of them, as I would tell you the names of the other figures if you asked me.
Meno: Courage and temperance and wisdom and magnanimity are virtues; and there are many others.
Socrates: Yes, Meno; and again we are in the same case: in searching after one virtue we have found many, though not in the same way as before; but we have been unable to find the common virtue which runs through them all.
Meno: Why, Socrates, even now I am not able to follow you in the attempt to get at one common notion of virtue as of other things.
Socrates: No wonder; but I will try to get nearer if I can, for you know that all things have a common notion. Suppose now that some one asked you the question which I asked before: Meno, he would say, what is figure? And if you answered "roundness," he would reply to you, in my way of speaking, by asking whether you would say that roundness is "figure" or "a figure"; and you would answer "a figure."
Meno: Certainly.

Here is the overall argumentation strategy: Socrates aims to prove the pre-existence of the soul by demonstrating that our knowledge of perfect, abstract concepts like 'absolute equality' must have been acquired before birth, as such perfection is not found in sensory experience.
Here are the conceded premises: What a man recollects he must have known at some previous time., Recollection can be triggered by perceiving something that reminds one of something else, even if the two are of different kinds of knowledge., The knowledge of a lyre is not the same as the knowledge of a man., Lovers recognize a lyre or garment and form an image of the beloved; this is recollection., Seeing Simmias can remind one of Cebes., Recollection is commonly recovering what has been forgotten., Recollection can be derived from things either like or unlike., When recollection is from like things, a consideration arises whether the likeness falls short of what is recollected.
Here is interlocutor profile: Simmias' current stance is one of agreement and willingness to follow Socrates' line of reasoning. He is receptive to Socrates' analogies and readily assents to the proposed definitions and examples of recollection. His recent behavior indicates a cooperative and agreeable participant, though he may require clarification on new or complex ideas.
Here is the dialogue summary: Socrates has introduced the concept of recollection and used several analogies (lyre, picture) to illustrate how one thing can remind us of another, whether like or unlike. Simmias has readily agreed to these preliminary points, establishing a foundational understanding of recollection as a process of recovering forgotten knowledge.
Here are the last lines of dialogue:
Socrates: And recollection is most commonly a process of recovering that which has been already forgotten through time and inattention.
Simmias: Very true.
Socrates: Well; and may you not also from seeing the picture of a horse or a lyre remember a man? and from the picture of Simmias, you may be led to remember Cebes?
Simmias: True.
Socrates: Or you may also be led to the recollection of Simmias himself?
Simmias: Quite so.
Socrates: And in all these cases, the recollection may be derived from things either like or unlike?
Simmias: It may be.
Socrates: And when the recollection is derived from like things, then another consideration is sure to arise, which is—whether the likeness in any degree falls short or not of that which is recollected?
Simmias: Very true.

Here is the overall argumentation strategy: Socrates aims to guide Meno towards understanding the requirements for a proper, universal definition of virtue by systematically eliciting, examining, and refuting Meno's inadequate initial attempts, and by providing methodological clarification through examples.
Here are the conceded premises: Bees do not differ from one another as bees., Health, size, and strength are the same whether in man or woman., Both men and women must have the same virtues of temperance and justice to be good., All men are good in the same way, by participation in the same virtues., Virtue is not the power of governing mankind if it includes children or slaves governing their superiors., Justice is a virtue., A 'figure' is a common nature that contains various specific figures like roundness and straightness., A 'color' is a common nature that contains various specific colors like whiteness.
Here is interlocutor profile: Meno's current task is to provide a universal definition of virtue. He is struggling to grasp the concept of a 'common notion' or universal essence, despite Socrates' analogies and direct questions. He has shown a tendency to provide lists of examples or definitions that are too narrow or circular, and he is now asking Socrates to provide the definition rather than attempting it himself, indicating a desire for Socrates to lead.
Here is the dialogue summary: Socrates has just provided a model definition of 'figure' and 'color' to illustrate the type of universal definition he is seeking for virtue. This followed Meno's difficulty in grasping the concept of a common essence after his second definition of virtue as 'the power of governing mankind' was refuted. Socrates is now pressing Meno to fulfill his promise to provide a universal definition of virtue, having demonstrated the method.
Here are the last lines of dialogue:
Socrates: You only assert that the round figure is not more a figure than the straight, or the straight than the round?
Meno: Very true.
Socrates: To what then do we give the name of figure? Try and answer. Suppose that when a person asked you this question either about figure or colour, you were to reply, Man, I do not understand what you want, or know what you are saying; he would look rather astonished and say: Do you not understand that I am looking for the "simile in multis"? And then he might put the question in another form: Mono, he might say, what is that "simile in multis" which you call figure, and which includes not only round and straight figures, but all? Could you not answer that question, Meno? I wish that you would try; the attempt will be good practice with a view to the answer about virtue.
Meno: I would rather that you should answer, Socrates.
Socrates: Shall I indulge you?
Meno: By all means.
Socrates: And then you will tell me about virtue?
Meno: I will.
Socrates: Then I must do my best, for there is a prize to be won.
Meno: Certainly.

Here is the overall argumentation strategy: Socrates aims to demonstrate that aptitudes for guardianship are distributed among individuals of both sexes, not exclusive to males, thereby justifying selection based on individual merit rather than gender.
Here are the conceded premises: A nature gifted or not gifted is distinguished by ease of learning, retention, and body's service to mind., The male sex generally possesses gifts and qualities in a higher degree than the female., There is no special faculty of administration unique to women or men by virtue of their sex., The gifts of nature are diffused alike in both sexes., All pursuits of men are also pursuits of women, but women are generally inferior in all of them.
Here is interlocutor profile: Glaucon currently holds that the male sex is generally superior to the female, though he acknowledges individual exceptions. He is cooperative and readily agrees to Socrates' definitions and observations.
Here is the dialogue summary: Socrates defined 'gifted by nature' and then prompted Glaucon to acknowledge the general inferiority of the female sex, which Glaucon readily affirmed. Socrates then used this concession to pivot to the idea that natural gifts are diffused among both sexes.
Here are the last lines of dialogue:
Socrates: And perhaps he, like yourself, will reply that to give a sufficient answer on the instant is not easy; but after a little reflection there is no difficulty.
Glaucon: Yes, perhaps.
Socrates: Suppose then that we invite him to accompany us in the argument, and then we may hope to show him that there is nothing peculiar in the constitution of women which would affect them in the administration of the State.
Glaucon: By all means.
Socrates: Let us say to him: Come now, and we will ask you a question: --when you spoke of a nature gifted or not gifted in any respect, did you mean to say that one man will acquire a thing easily, another with difficulty; a little learning will lead the one to discover a great deal; whereas the other, after much study and application, no sooner learns than he forgets; or again, did you mean, that the one has a body which is a good servant to his mind, while the body of the other is a hindrance to him?-would not these be the sort of differences which distinguish the man gifted by nature from the one who is ungifted?
Glaucon: No one will deny that.
Socrates: And can you mention any pursuit of mankind in which the male sex has not all these gifts and qualities in a higher degree than the female? Need I waste time in speaking of the art of weaving, and the management of pancakes and preserves, in which womankind does really appear to be great, and in which for her to be beaten by a man is of all things the most absurd?
Glaucon: You are quite right in maintaining the general inferiority of the female sex: although many women are in many things superior to many men, yet on the whole what you say is true.
Socrates: And if so, my friend, there is no special faculty of administration in a state which a woman has because she is a woman, or which a man has by virtue of his sex, but the gifts of nature are alike diffused in both; all the pursuits of men are the pursuits of women also, but in all of them a woman is inferior to a man.
Glaucon: Very true.
